summary: Children ages 9–11 learn that adaptations are features or behaviours that help an animal survive in its environment, classified as structural (body parts), behavioural (things it does) or physiological (internal/chemical processes), and that adaptations arise over many generations by natural selection — not within one animal's lifetime through willing, trying or use. The load-bearing idea, and the one most prone to the Lamarckian misconception, is the over-generations mechanism: pre-existing variation filtered by differential survival and reproduction.
misconceptions: 'Animals change their bodies to fit their needs / because they want to or try hard' (Lamarckism) — adaptations are selected over generations, not willed or grown in a lifetime.
'An individual adapts during its life' — individuals may acclimatise, but adaptation of the species happens across generations.
'Adaptation and evolution are the same thing' — adaptation is fit-to-environment; accumulated adaptation via selection is a mechanism of evolution.
'Only physical body parts are adaptations' — behaviours and internal/chemical processes are adaptations too.
'Natural selection has a goal / animals evolve to become better/more advanced' — selection is non-purposive filtering of existing variation by survival and reproduction.

activities.title: Run a population across generations: selection sandbox
steps: Seed a habitat with a population of animals that VARY in one inherited trait that matters for survival — for example body colour of prey against the ground, or beak size of seed-eating birds for the available seeds.
Choose the environment (e.g. dark soil vs pale sand; large hard seeds vs small soft seeds).

Apply an environmental pressure — a predator that more easily catches poorly-camouflaged prey, or a food source only certain beaks can handle — so poorly-suited individuals are more likely to die or leave fewer offspring.
Let the survivors reproduce, passing on their traits with fresh variation in the offspring.
Watch a trait-frequency graph update each generation and describe how the proportion of the well-suited trait changes.
Use a control toggle that freezes reproduction and follows ONE animal through its whole life; confirm that single individual never grows a new adaptation.
State in your own words what changed (the population) and what did not (any individual).
activities.insight: The population shifts toward the well-suited trait over generations while no individual's inherited trait changes: adaptation is pre-existing variation filtered by survival and reproduction across generations, not a feature an animal grows because it tries or needs to.

activities.title: Sort real adaptations into three kinds
steps: Sort many real example cards into three columns: structural (body parts), behavioural (things the animal does), physiological (internal/chemical processes).

Place examples such as giraffe's long neck, eagle's talons and dolphin's streamlined body under structural; migration, hibernation and tool use under behavioural; antifreeze proteins in Arctic fish blood, bat echolocation and venom under physiological.
For each card, say WHAT KIND of adaptation it is and justify why (is it a body part, a behaviour, or an internal process?).
Flag any example you think belongs in more than one column and explain your reasoning.
activities.insight: Adaptations are not only physical body parts; behaviours and internal/chemical processes are adaptations too, and reasoning about the KIND directs attention to the underlying category rather than a memorised definition.

activities.title: Match each adaptation to the survival problem it solves
steps: For several animals, pair a feature or behaviour with the specific survival PROBLEM and environment it addresses (e.g. streamlined body ↔ moving fast through water; hibernation ↔ surviving a season with little food).
For each pairing, name the environment and the problem explicitly, then state how the adaptation helps the animal survive and reproduce.
Compare two animals in different environments and explain why a trait that helps in one setting may not help in another.
activities.insight: 'Adaptation' means fit-to-environment — a feature that solves a specific survival problem in a particular setting — not just 'a cool feature'.

activities.title: Beaks-and-foods investigation: why varied traits survive in different niches
steps: Use different tools as 'beaks' — e.g. tweezers, pliers, a spoon — and a mix of 'foods' such as dried seeds, rubber-band 'worms', and water.
Before timing, PREDICT which beak will collect the most of each food type.
Collect each food for a fixed time and record how much each beak gathered.
Compare predictions with results and identify which beak 'wins' with which food.
Explain what this shows about why varied beak shapes can each survive in different niches, and why no single beak is best at everything.
activities.insight: Different beaks win with different foods: varied traits are the raw material selection acts on, and the best trait depends on the environment, so there is no single 'best' design.

activities.title: The giraffe neck: diagnose and explain how the trait arose
steps: Read this claim from a student: 'Giraffes got long necks because they kept stretching to reach higher leaves, and passed those longer necks on to their babies.'
Decide whether this is how it happened, and if not, explain how giraffes came to have long necks.

Answer probing follow-ups: Did ONE giraffe's neck get longer, or did giraffe necks get longer over generations — what's the difference? Where did the variation (some giraffes with longer necks than others) come from in the first place? A bodybuilder gets big muscles by training — will their baby be born with big muscles, and what does that tell us about how neck length is passed on?
Also decide: is hibernation an adaptation even though it isn't a body part? Why?
activities.insight: Adaptation arises across generations by natural selection on inherited variation: in a widely taught explanation, some giraffes happened to have slightly longer necks, those reached more food, survived better and had more young, so over many generations the average neck grew longer — distinct from an individual acquiring a trait by stretching and passing on what it gained.

activities.title: In-role field biologist: probe your 'why does it have that?' reasoning (optional)
steps: Explain to an in-role field biologist (or naturalist) WHY an animal has a particular feature or behaviour.
Respond to Socratic follow-ups that press on how the trait arose — over a lifetime or over generations — and on whether the animal intended it.
Revise your explanation to describe variation, differential survival and reproduction across generations.
activities.insight: Articulating and defending a causal explanation out loud can surface hidden Lamarckian or intentional assumptions and lets the learner rebuild the account in terms of selection.

checkQuestion: Giraffes have very long necks that let them reach leaves high in the trees. A student says: 'Giraffes got long necks because they kept stretching to reach higher leaves, and passed those longer necks on to their babies.' Is that how it happened? If not, how did giraffes come to have long necks?
checkAnswer: That isn't how it works — stretching during one giraffe's life doesn't lengthen its babies' necks. In the past giraffes varied: some happened to have slightly longer necks than others. Those could reach more food, survived better and had more young, passing on the genes for longer necks. Over many, many generations the average neck grew longer. The change happens across generations by natural selection acting on inherited variation, not by an individual stretching and passing on what it gained.
